who: Joseph was the eleventh son of Jacob, in the book of Genesis. He is not Joseph of Nazareth, the husband of Mary. His jealous brothers sold him into slavery in Egypt. He rose from prison to rule Egypt under Pharaoh, after reading his dreams. In the famine his brothers came to him for grain, and he forgave them.

tidbits.text: Matthew's Joseph, the husband of Mary, was also a son of a Jacob. He too was led by dreams, and took his family down to Egypt.
Tertullian, writing about 197, told the pagans that their god Serapis was Joseph. The god's headdress was shaped like a grain measure, he said, and “marks the memory of his corn-provisioning”.
Jesus met the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, by “the plot of ground that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.”
Ambrose praised him for selling the grain, not giving it away: “For if he had given it to a few there would have been none for most.”

cite.text: Ambrose, *On the Duties of the Clergy*, book 2, chapter 16

facts.label: Name
facts.text: **Joseph** sounds like the Hebrew for **may He add**. His mother named him with a prayer: “May the LORD add to me another son.”

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Zaphenath-paneah**, the Egyptian name Pharaoh gave him. **Joseph the Fair**, or **the All-Comely**, in the Orthodox Church. He is not **Joseph of Nazareth**, Mary's husband.

facts.label: Parents
facts.text: **Jacob**, also called Israel, and **Rachel**, the wife Jacob loved. She died giving birth to his brother **Benjamin**.

facts.label: Brothers
facts.text: He was the **eleventh** of Jacob's **twelve** sons. Ten were his half-brothers, sons of Leah and of two maidservants.

facts.label: Born
facts.text: In **Paddan-aram**, where Jacob worked for his uncle Laban. He grew up in **Canaan**.

facts.label: When
facts.text: Genesis gives no year. Moses was the great-grandson of Joseph's brother **Levi**. The OCA dates Joseph's death to about **1700 BC**.

facts.label: Wife and sons
facts.text: **Asenath**, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. Their sons **Manasseh** and **Ephraim** each became a tribe of Israel.

facts.label: Languages
facts.text: He spoke to his brothers through an **interpreter**, though he understood every word they said.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: No book. His words are kept in Genesis 37 to 50.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: In **Egypt**, at **110**. His bones were buried at last at **Shechem**, in Canaan.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: The robe and the pit, Potiphar's wife clutching his cloak, Pharaoh's dreams, and the brothers bowing before him.

east.text: **Righteous Joseph the Patriarch**, in the **OCA**. The Orthodox keep him again on **Great and Holy Monday**, the Monday of Holy Week, and on the **Sunday of the Holy Fathers** before Christmas.

quotes.q: Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him and rescued him from all his troubles. He granted Joseph favor and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt, who appointed him ruler over Egypt and all his household.
quotes.who: Stephen, on trial before the council in Jerusalem, shortly before he was stoned.

quotes.q: He sent a man before them—Joseph, sold as a slave. They bruised his feet with shackles and placed his neck in irons, until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right.
quotes.who: Psalm 105, singing of what God did for Israel.

quotes.q: Nor was there a man born like Joseph, a leader of his kindred, a supporter of the people. Even his bones were cared for.
quotes.who: Ben Sira, in the book of Sirach. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles hold it; most Protestant Bibles leave it out, or print it among the Apocrypha.

quotes.q: Envy made Joseph be persecuted unto death, and to come into bondage.
quotes.who: Clement of Rome, writing to Corinth about 97, on what envy does.

quotes.q: He who is enamoured of chastity dwells upon the history of Joseph, and from him learns chaste actions.
quotes.who: Basil the Great, writing to his friend Gregory about why we read the lives of holy men.

quotes.q: How meek he was in slavery, how unchanging in virtue, how kindly in prison! Wise, too, in interpreting, and self-restrained in exercising his power!
quotes.who: Ambrose of Milan, in his book of advice for his clergy, about 391.

cite.text: Ambrose, *On the Duties of the Clergy*, book 1, chapter 24

quotes.q: Who then before Moses was patient? The blessed and noble Joseph, who having shone by his chastity, shone no less by his long suffering.

moments.title: The robe and the dreams
moments.text: Joseph was Jacob's favourite, the son of his old age, born to his beloved Rachel. At seventeen he brought his father a bad report about his brothers. Jacob “made him a robe of many colors”, and his brothers “hated him and could not speak a kind word to him.” Then Joseph dreamed that their sheaves of grain bowed down to his sheaf. In a second dream “the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me.” Even Jacob rebuked him. Yet “his father kept in mind what he had said.”

moments.title: Into the pit
moments.text: Jacob sent him to see how his brothers and the flocks were doing. They saw him coming. “Here comes that dreamer!” they said. “Come now, let us kill him.” Reuben talked them into throwing him into a pit instead, meaning to rescue him later. They stripped off his robe, threw him into the dry pit, and sat down to eat. When a caravan came by on its way to Egypt, Judah said, “What profit will we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood?” They sold him for twenty shekels of silver.

moments.title: The robe in the blood
moments.text: When Reuben came back to the pit, it was empty. “The boy is gone! What am I going to do?” The brothers killed a young goat and dipped Joseph's robe in its blood. They sent it to their father: “Examine it to see whether it is your son's robe or not.” Jacob knew it at once. “Joseph has surely been torn to pieces!” He tore his clothes and would not be comforted. “I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son.”

moments.title: A slave who prospered
moments.text: The traders sold him to Potiphar, the captain of Pharaoh's guard. “And the LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man.” Potiphar saw it, and put him in charge of everything he owned. From then on the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house because of Joseph. Potiphar concerned himself with nothing “except the food he ate.”

moments.title: He left his cloak
moments.text: Joseph was “well-built and handsome”, and his master's wife wanted him. Day after day she asked him to sleep with her. He refused: “So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?” One day, with no servants in the house, she grabbed him by his cloak. He left it in her hand and ran outside. She showed the cloak to the servants, then to her husband, and said the Hebrew slave had come to mock her. Potiphar burned with anger, and had Joseph thrown into the king's prison.

moments.title: The cupbearer and the baker
moments.text: Even there, “the LORD was with him”, and the warden put all the prisoners in his care. Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker were thrown in with him. One morning both were downcast: each had dreamed, and no one could tell them what it meant. “Don't interpretations belong to God?” Joseph said. The cupbearer's three branches meant that in three days he would have his post back. The baker's three baskets meant that in three days he would be hanged. It happened just so, on Pharaoh's birthday. Joseph had asked the cupbearer to remember him. But the cupbearer “forgot all about him.”

moments.title: Pharaoh's dreams
moments.text: Pharaoh dreamed that seven thin cows ate up seven fat ones, and that seven thin heads of grain swallowed seven full ones. None of his magicians could explain it. Then the cupbearer remembered. Joseph was brought out of the dungeon, shaved and changed. “I myself cannot do it,” he said, “but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer.” Seven years of plenty were coming, then seven years of famine. Let Pharaoh set a wise man over the land, and store a fifth of the harvest in the good years.

moments.title: Over all the land of Egypt
moments.text: “Can we find anyone like this man,” Pharaoh asked, “in whom the Spirit of God abides?” He put his own signet ring on Joseph's finger, dressed him in fine linen and hung a gold chain around his neck. Men ran before his chariot calling, “Bow the knee!” Pharaoh gave him an Egyptian name, Zaphenath-paneah, and a wife, Asenath. Joseph was thirty. In the seven good years he stored up grain “like the sand of the sea”, until he stopped counting.

moments.title: The brothers bow
moments.text: The famine reached Canaan, and Jacob sent ten of his sons to Egypt for grain. He kept Benjamin, Rachel's other son, at home. The brothers came before the governor and “bowed down before him with their faces to the ground.” Joseph knew them, but they did not know him. He remembered his dreams. “You are spies!” he said, and held them for three days. Then, not knowing he understood, they said to one another, “Surely we are being punished because of our brother.” Joseph turned away and wept. He kept Simeon bound, and sent the rest home with grain and their silver hidden in their sacks.

moments.title: Benjamin and the silver cup
moments.text: When the grain ran out, Jacob let Benjamin go. Seeing his mother's son, Joseph hurried out of the room to weep, then washed his face and came back. At dinner Benjamin's portion was five times larger than anyone else's. Then Joseph had his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack, and sent his steward after them. The cup was found, and they all came back. Judah pleaded for the boy: their father would die if he did not come home. “Now please let your servant stay here as my lord's slave in place of the boy.”

moments.title: “I am Joseph!”
moments.text: Joseph could hold back no longer. He sent everyone else out, and wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard. “I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?” His brothers were too terrified to answer. “Please come near me,” he said. “It was not you who sent me here, but God.” He threw his arms around Benjamin and wept, and kissed each of his brothers. As they left to fetch their father, he told them, “Do not quarrel on the way!”

moments.title: Father and son
moments.text: At first Jacob did not believe it. Then he saw the wagons Joseph had sent. “My son Joseph is still alive! I will go to see him before I die.” On the way God spoke to him at Beersheba: “Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt.” Seventy of the family went down in all. Joseph drove out to Goshen to meet his father, threw his arms around him and wept. “Finally I can die,” said Israel, “now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!”

moments.title: Grain for land
moments.text: The famine grew worse. The Egyptians spent all their money on Joseph's grain, then traded him their livestock. At last they offered their land and themselves, for seed to sow. So all the land of Egypt became Pharaoh's, except the priests' land, and Joseph “reduced the people to servitude from one end of Egypt to the other.” From then on they gave Pharaoh a fifth of every harvest. “You have saved our lives,” they told him.

moments.title: The crossed hands
moments.text: Jacob fell ill, and Joseph brought his two sons to be blessed. He set Manasseh, the elder, at his father's right hand. Jacob crossed his arms and laid his right hand on Ephraim, the younger. Joseph tried to move it. “Not so, my father!” he said. “This one is the firstborn.” “I know, my son, I know!” Jacob answered, and put Ephraim first. On his deathbed he blessed Joseph as “a fruitful vine by a spring, whose branches scale the wall.”

moments.title: What they meant for evil
moments.text: Jacob was buried in Canaan, in the cave where Abraham lay. Then the brothers were afraid. “What if Joseph bears a grudge?” They sent word that their father had asked Joseph to forgive them. Joseph wept. They came and fell down before him: “We are your slaves!” He answered, “Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?” God had meant it all for good, he told them. “I will provide for you and your little ones.”

extras.title: A picture of Christ
extras.lede: The early Church read Joseph's story as a picture of Christ's. The Orthodox still do, at the start of Holy Week.

items.title: Hated by his own
items.text: Stephen told Joseph's story to the council that condemned him (Acts 7). John Chrysostom, preaching on that speech, saw Christ in it. His brothers had no fault to find with Joseph, he said,
items.quote: and though he came on purpose to bring them their food, they thus ill-treated him.

cite.text: Acts 7:9; John Chrysostom, *Homilies on Acts*, Homily 17

items.title: Sold for silver
items.text: His brothers took twenty shekels of silver for him. Judas was paid thirty for Jesus. Ambrose of Milan set the two sales side by side: “In one place the sale is for twenty pieces, in the other for thirty.”
items.quote: Joseph was sold, Jesus Christ was bought, the one to slavery, the Other to death.

cite.text: Genesis 37:28; Matthew 26:15; Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book 3, chapter 17

items.title: Silent when accused
items.text: Potiphar's wife lied about him, and Genesis gives him no word in his own defence. John Chrysostom saw the Passion in it:
items.quote: What then did Joseph? He held his peace, and thus is condemned, even as Christ is also.

cite.text: Genesis 39:13-20; John Chrysostom, *Homilies on Matthew*, Homily 84

items.title: Holy Monday
items.text: The Orthodox begin Holy Week with him. On Great and Holy Monday they remember Joseph the All-Comely, beside the fig tree that Jesus cursed. A Russian Orthodox priest in Texas lists the likenesses for his parish: sold for silver, thrown into a pit, patient under wrong, and feeding his people with bread.

cite.text: Priest Seraphim Holland, “Joseph the All-Comely, a type of Christ”, 2010; OCA, Righteous Joseph the Patriarch

words.note: He wrote nothing. His words are kept in Genesis. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible. The exceptions are Sirach, from the World English Bible, and one King James line, named where it stands.

feature.kicker: To his brothers, after their father's death
feature.q: As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people.
feature.ctx: They had fallen down before him: “We are your slaves!” He wept, and first told them, “Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?”

quotes.q: So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?
quotes.who: To Potiphar's wife, who asked him day after day.

quotes.q: Don't interpretations belong to God? Tell me your dreams.
quotes.who: In prison, to Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker.

quotes.q: But when it goes well for you, please remember me and show me kindness by mentioning me to Pharaoh, that he might bring me out of this prison.
quotes.who: To the cupbearer, who then forgot him for two full years.

quotes.q: God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.
quotes.who: Naming his second son, Ephraim. The first he named Manasseh: “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father's household.”

quotes.q: I am Joseph, your brother, the one you sold into Egypt! And now, do not be distressed or angry with yourselves that you sold me into this place, because it was to save lives that God sent me before you.
quotes.who: Making himself known to his brothers.

quotes.q: Do not quarrel on the way!
quotes.who: His parting words to his brothers, as they left to fetch their father.

myths.claim: Jacob gave Joseph a coat of many colours.
myths.truth: Perhaps. The King James Version reads “a coat of many colours”, and the BSB keeps “a robe of many colors”. But no one is sure what the Hebrew word means. It is found only here and in 2 Samuel 13, for the robe of King David's daughter Tamar, “because this is what the king's virgin daughters wore.” *Strong's* gives its first sense as the palm of the hand or the sole of the foot. So it may have been a robe reaching to the wrists and ankles, “a long and sleeved tunic”.

cite.text: Genesis 37:3, BSB and King James Version; 2 Samuel 13:18; Strong's Hebrew 6446, at Bible Hub

myths.truth: Genesis never names her. The name comes from later Arab tellings of the story, where she is Zulaikha. A Hebrew retelling, the *Sefer ha-Yashar*, took the name over as Zelikah, “following Arabic sources”, says the *Jewish Encyclopedia*.

An old guess. Gregory of Tours, writing in the 500s, said Joseph built “wonderful granaries of squared stone and rubble” in Egypt, wide at the base and narrow at the top, “and these granaries are to be seen at the present day.” Some Arab writers also said he built the pyramids. Genesis says only that he stored the grain “in the cities”. The pyramids were built as tombs for Egypt's kings.

cite.text: Genesis 41:48; Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book 1, chapter 10; *Jewish Encyclopedia*, “Joseph”

circle.name: Moses
circle.text: Born generations later, the great-grandson of Joseph's brother Levi. When Israel left Egypt, he carried Joseph's bones with him, as Joseph had made them swear.

circle.name: Jacob
circle.text: His father, also called Israel. He loved Joseph more than his other sons, and mourned him for twenty-two years. He came down to Egypt to see him before he died.

circle.name: Rachel
circle.text: His mother, the wife Jacob loved, childless for years. “God has taken away my shame,” she said when Joseph was born. She died on the road to Bethlehem, giving birth to Benjamin.

circle.name: Benjamin
circle.text: His only full brother, the youngest of the twelve. Joseph's silver cup was hidden in his sack. Joseph gave him three hundred shekels of silver and five sets of clothes.

circle.name: Reuben
circle.text: The eldest brother. He talked the others out of killing Joseph and meant to rescue him. Years later, in Egypt, he reminded them: “Didn't I tell you not to sin against the boy?”

circle.name: Judah
circle.text: The brother who said, “Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites.” Years later he offered himself as a slave in Benjamin's place.

circle.name: Potiphar
circle.text: An officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, who bought Joseph and put him over his house. He believed his wife, and sent Joseph to prison.

circle.name: Potiphar's wife
circle.text: Genesis never names her. When Joseph would not sleep with her, she kept his cloak and accused him.

circle.name: Pharaoh
circle.text: The king whose dreams Joseph read. He set Joseph over all Egypt: “Only with regard to the throne will I be greater than you.”

circle.name: Asenath, Manasseh and Ephraim
circle.text: His Egyptian wife, a priest's daughter, and their two sons. Jacob counted the boys as his own, and each became a tribe of Israel.

death.big: He died in Egypt at 110, and made his family swear to carry his bones home.
paras: He lived long. “He saw Ephraim's sons to the third generation, and indeed the sons of Machir son of Manasseh were brought up on Joseph's knees.” Then he called his brothers.
“So Joseph died at the age of 110. And they embalmed his body and placed it in a coffin in Egypt.” It is the last line of Genesis.

Generations later a new king came to power, “who did not know Joseph”. When Israel left Egypt at last, “Moses took the bones of Joseph with him”. They were buried at Shechem, in the field Jacob had bought, and it became the inheritance of Joseph's descendants.
The letter to the Hebrews counts it as faith: “By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones.”

items.k: To his brothers, as he was dying
items.q: I am about to die, but God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land He promised on oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

items.k: The oath he made them swear
items.q: God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place.

later.title: A coffin in the Nile
later.text: Jewish tradition tells more. Most of the rabbis held that his coffin was sunk in the Nile, says the *Jewish Encyclopedia*. At the Exodus, Serah, daughter of Asher, showed Moses the place. Moses threw a pebble into the water and called Joseph by name, and the coffin floated up.

saint.big: Yes, in the Orthodox Church, which keeps him as Righteous Joseph on 31 March and again in Holy Week. Rome gives him no day of his own. Lutherans in the Missouri Synod remember him on 31 March.

churches.note: 31 March, and Great and Holy Monday
Church of England and Episcopal Church

paras: The OCA calls him Righteous Joseph, and Joseph the Fair. As the father of Manasseh and Ephraim, it notes, he stands at the head of two of the tribes of Israel.
Rome's book of martyrs, in its 1916 edition and in the edition of 2004, has no entry for him. The Missouri Synod remembers him for his uprightness and for forgiving his brothers.
Long before any calendar, Tertullian was already counting him among the saints. Writing about 197, he told the pagans:

quotes.q: For that Serapis of yours was originally one of our own saints called Joseph.
quotes.who: Tertullian, claiming the Egyptian god Serapis as Joseph in disguise

kin.text: Like Joseph, a young Hebrew carried off to a foreign court. He told a king what his dream meant, saying, “there is a God in heaven Who reveals mysteries”, and was made ruler over a province.

kin.name: Esther
kin.text: Like Joseph, raised up in a foreign palace, where her place saved her people. “Who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”
